lesson.title: Power from batteries and the sun
lesson.subtitle: Why the radio eats the battery, and how the sun keeps a sensor going

video.title: Power from batteries and the sun
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Amina Bello — teacher who runs the school garden club, the student's teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Mr Okafor — science teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Amina in the school garden holding a small sensor box and a phone showing live readings; then the phone shows 'offline'.
scenes.animation: Readings tick up every second; the battery icon drains fast and goes grey.
scenes.narration: Our garden sensor sent a reading over Wi-Fi every ten seconds, so we could watch it live. It was exciting, for four days. Then two brand-new batteries were flat. Today, you'll learn to make them last for years.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Power from batteries and the sun
scenes.narration: Today: power from batteries and the sun, and why the radio eats the battery.

scenes.visual: Two AA batteries drawn as a small water tank; taps labelled sleep, measure and send drip from it.
scenes.animation: The tank level falls as the taps drip.
scenes.on_screen_text: A battery is a tank of charge
scenes.narration: Think of a battery as a tank of charge, measured in milliamp-hours. Two AA batteries hold about two thousand five hundred. Every part of the device drinks from that tank, and its life in hours is the capacity divided by the average current.

scenes.visual: Three bars: sleep (too small to see), measure (short), Wi-Fi send (towering).
scenes.animation: Bars grow as each is said; the send bar shoots off the top.
scenes.narration: Now compare. Asleep, a sensor uses about a hundredth of a milliamp. Measuring takes about five milliamps, for a tenth of a second. Sending over Wi-Fi takes about one hundred and twenty milliamps, for two seconds. One Wi-Fi send uses as much as nearly seven hours of sleep!

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at his desk with the garden sensor open beside a laptop. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A sensor sends every ten seconds, and its batteries last four days. What makes the biggest difference: sending less often, or sleeping more deeply?

scenes.visual: Split screen: a battery draining in days beside one that stays nearly full through a calendar of years.
scenes.animation: Calendar pages flip on the right while the left battery empties.
scenes.narration: Send less often. Every ten seconds, the radio takes almost all the energy. Send once an hour instead, and the same two batteries can last more than three years.

scenes.visual: A sleeping sensor box with a small 'z' wakes, blinks, sends one burst, and dozes off again.
scenes.animation: Long sleeps, short blinks; then ten readings bundle into one envelope.
scenes.narration: So a good sensor sleeps almost all the time. It wakes, measures, sends, and goes straight back to sleep. It can also save ten readings and send them together, or send only when something changes.

scenes.visual: A sensor on a pole in the school garden with a palm-sized solar panel on top and a battery box below; day turns to night.
scenes.animation: Sunlight fills the battery; at dusk the flow reverses from battery to sensor.
scenes.on_screen_text: Sun by day, battery by night
scenes.narration: Outdoors, add a small solar panel and a rechargeable battery. By day, the panel runs the sensor and charges the battery. At night, the battery takes over. Much of Africa and the Middle East gets four to six hours of strong sun a day.

scenes.visual: A week of weather icons: three suns, then five clouds; a battery gauge falls through the cloudy days and refills when the sun returns.
scenes.animation: The gauge steps down day by day, then climbs back.
scenes.narration: Then plan for cloudy days. Say your sensor uses one hundred milliamp-hours a day. The battery should carry it through five cloudy days, so five hundred, plus extra, because no battery gives all of its label. And on sunny days, the panel must refill it too.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor beside a rain sensor on a pole at dusk; its light goes out as the sun sets. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Why does it stop at night?
scenes.narration: Your turn. A solar-powered rain sensor works all day, but stops every night. What's most likely wrong?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: a radio wave, a sleeping box, a sun, a cloud.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The battery: at night, only the battery keeps the sensor going. Remember: the radio is the hungriest part. Sleep most of the time, and send less often. And outdoors: sun by day, a battery by night, sized for cloudy days.

scenes.visual: A student reads the label on a power bank and works out a sum in a notebook.
scenes.animation: The label zooms in on '10000 mAh'; the sum writes itself.
scenes.narration: Try it this week: find the milliamp-hours on a power bank or a battery label. Work out how many hours it could run a device drawing one hundred milliamps, then ten. And never crush, pierce or leave a lithium battery in hot sun.

checkpoints.prompt: A sensor sends every 10 seconds; its batteries last 4 days. What makes the biggest difference?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — sending takes almost all the energy, so sending less often makes the biggest difference.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — sleep already uses only about 0.01 mA. The radio takes almost all the energy, so send less often.

checkpoints.prompt: A solar-powered sensor works all day but stops every night. What's most likely wrong?

options.text: The battery is too small or worn out

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the panel works, because it runs the sensor all day. At night only the battery runs it, so the battery isn't holding enough.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the panel must be working, because the sensor runs all day. At night only the battery runs it, so check the battery.
